questions.q: For which class of joint distributions does linear (Pearson) correlation fully describe the dependence structure?
options: Any joint distribution whatsoever
Jointly elliptical distributions, such as the multivariate normal
Only distributions with zero mean
Only distributions observed over exactly one year
questions.explain: Correlation fully summarizes dependence for jointly elliptical distributions like the multivariate normal; real asset returns often depart from this, which is where tail dependence becomes relevant.

options: The average correlation over the full sample
A tendency for extreme moves in one variable to coincide with extreme moves in another far more (or less) often than a correlation-matched normal distribution would predict
The portion of a time series near its endpoints
A measure of how fat a single variable's own marginal tail is, ignoring any other variable
questions.explain: Tail dependence describes joint extreme behavior between variables -- specifically how it compares to what the same linear correlation would imply under a normal distribution.

questions.q: What does Sklar's theorem say, stated informally?
options: All joint distributions are multivariate normal
Any joint distribution can be split into each variable's own marginal distribution plus a copula describing how their percentile ranks move together
Correlation cannot be computed for non-normal data
Marginals and dependence structure cannot be separated
questions.explain: Sklar's theorem (informally) says a joint distribution decomposes into the individual marginals and a copula capturing the pure dependence structure between them.

questions.q: In the worked example, both the Gaussian copula and Student-t copula pairs were built with the same linear correlation (rho=0.5, verified empirically at ~0.49-0.50). What differed between them at the 1% joint tail?
options: Nothing differed; results were identical
The Gaussian copula had a higher joint tail probability than the t-copula
The Student-t copula's joint tail probability (0.00278) was more than double the Gaussian copula's (0.00133), despite matching linear correlation
Only the Gaussian copula could be simulated at all
questions.explain: Even with matching linear correlation, the t-copula produced a joint tail probability of 0.00278 at q=0.01, versus 0.00133 for the Gaussian copula -- more than double, demonstrating positive tail dependence.

questions.q: Why did the Gaussian copula's joint tail probabilities (0.01212 at q=0.05, 0.00133 at q=0.01) closely match the directly simulated bivariate normal's values (0.01192 and 0.00130)?
options: This was a coincidence with no underlying reason
Because the Gaussian copula is constructed from a multivariate normal distribution, so it should reproduce the same joint tail behavior as a direct bivariate normal draw at matching correlation
Because both used the same random seed by mistake
Because the Student-t copula was used for both
questions.explain: The Gaussian copula is built from correlated standard normals mapped through the normal CDF, so it inherits the multivariate normal's exact tail behavior -- a useful consistency check in the worked example.
